# Reproducible report and data description

## Introduction

This report uses a synthetic student-performance dataset to examine the relationship between students' final scores and three predictors: study hours per week (study_hours_per_week), attendance percentage (attendance_pct), and prior academic score (prior_score). The response variable is final_score. The objective is to apply NumPy matrix operations to fit a linear regression model using least squares and evaluate its numerical properties through matrix rank, QR decomposition, singular value decomposition (SVD), and condition-number diagnostics. Since the dataset is synthetic, the analysis focuses on statistical associations rather than causal relationships.

## Data inspection and validation

## Reproducibility

This report reads the supplied CSV through a relative path, executes all calculations from the source data, and generates numerical results directly from Python. It does not depend on hidden notebook state or manually entered results.

# Matrix setup and standardization

```{python}
predictor_cols = [
    "study_hours_per_week",
    "attendance_pct",
    "prior_score",
]
response_col = "final_score"

predictors = df[predictor_cols].to_numpy(dtype=float)
y = df[response_col].to_numpy(dtype=float)

# NumPy uses ddof=0 by default; this matches the homework specification.
means = predictors.mean(axis=0)
sds = predictors.std(axis=0)
assert np.all(sds > 0), "At least one predictor has zero standard deviation."
Z = (predictors - means) / sds

X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Z)), Z])

print("Predictor means:", means)
print("Predictor standard deviations:", sds)
print("Z.mean(axis=0):", Z.mean(axis=0))
print("Z.std(axis=0):", Z.std(axis=0))
print("predictors.shape:", predictors.shape)
print("Z.shape:", Z.shape)
print("X.shape:", X.shape)
print("y.shape:", y.shape)
print("Matrix rank of X:", np.linalg.matrix_rank(X))
print("Number of predictors (excluding intercept):", predictors.shape[1])
```


The predictor matrix has dimensions `{python} predictors.shape`, while the response vector has shape `{python} y.shape`, ensuring that each observation has a corresponding response value. Adding a column of ones produces a design matrix of shape `{python} X.shape`, allowing the regression model to estimate an intercept alongside the three predictor coefficients. Standardization centers each predictor around zero and scales it to have a standard deviation of one, making the predictors comparable despite their different measurement units. NumPy broadcasting performs this operation by subtracting the vector of column means and dividing by the vector of column standard deviations without requiring an explicit Python loop. The resulting standardized predictors have means approximately equal to zero and standard deviations equal to one, confirming that the transformation was successful.

# Least squares

```{python}
beta_hat, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
coefficient_names = ["Intercept"] + [f"Standardized: {col}" for col in predictor_cols]
coefficients = pd.Series(beta_hat, index=coefficient_names, name="Estimate")
print("Least-squares estimated coefficients:")
display(coefficients.to_frame())

largest_idx = np.argmax(np.abs(beta_hat[1:]))
print("Predictor with largest absolute standardized coefficient:", predictor_cols[largest_idx])

fitted = X @ beta_hat
residuals = y - fitted
rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean(residuals ** 2))

print("Mean residual:", residuals.mean())
print("RMSE:", rmse)
print("Elementwise X * beta_hat shape:", (X * beta_hat).shape)
print("Matrix product X @ beta_hat shape:", fitted.shape)
```

The least-squares coefficients were estimated using `np.linalg.lstsq()`, and the matrix multiplication `X @ beta_hat` generates the fitted final scores. Among the standardized predictors, `{python} predictor_cols[largest_idx]` has the largest absolute estimated coefficient, indicating the largest fitted change in final score for a one-standard-deviation increase in a predictor, holding the others constant. The mean residual is approximately zero because the regression model includes an intercept, which causes the ordinary least-squares residuals to sum to zero up to numerical rounding. The in-sample RMSE is `{python} f"{rmse:.2f}"`, measured in final-score units, and summarizes the magnitude of the differences between observed and fitted scores. Finally, `*` performs elementwise multiplication using broadcasting, whereas `@` performs matrix multiplication and produces a vector of fitted values.

# QR, SVD, and conditioning

## QR decomposition

```{python}
Q, R = np.linalg.qr(X)
print("Q.shape:", Q.shape)
print("R.shape:", R.shape)
print("Q @ R is close to X:", np.allclose(Q @ R, X))
print("Q.T @ Q is close to I:", np.allclose(Q.T @ Q, np.eye(Q.shape[1])))
```

## Singular value decomposition

```{python}
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X, full_matrices=False)
print("U.shape:", U.shape)
print("s.shape:", s.shape)
print("Vt.shape:", Vt.shape)
print("Singular values:", s)

X_reconstructed = U @ np.diag(s) @ Vt
print("SVD reconstruction close to X:", np.allclose(X_reconstructed, X))
```

## Rank and conditioning

```{python}
X_raw = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(predictors)), predictors])
cond_raw = np.linalg.cond(X_raw)
cond_standardized = np.linalg.cond(X)
print("rank of standardized X:", np.linalg.matrix_rank(X))
print("condition number of standardized X:", cond_standardized)
print("condition number of raw X:", cond_raw)
```


The QR reconstruction check returned `True`, confirming that multiplying $Q$ and $R$ reproduces the standardized design matrix $X$ within numerical tolerance. The orthogonality check also returned `True`, verifying that the columns of $Q$ are orthonormal because $Q^\top Q \approx I$. Similarly, the SVD reconstruction was successful, and the singular values describe the strength of the design matrix along different directions, with very small singular values potentially indicating near-linear dependence. A large condition number suggests that matrix computations may be sensitive to small perturbations or numerical errors. The condition number decreased from `{python} f"{cond_raw:.2f}"` for the raw design matrix to `{python} f"{cond_standardized:.2f}"` after standardization. This considerable reduction suggests that differences in the original predictors' measurement scales contributed substantially to the raw matrix's poor conditioning. Since the standardized design matrix has full column rank and a relatively low condition number, there is no evidence of severe near-redundancy among its columns, although standardization cannot eliminate genuine multicollinearity.

# Reproducibility and numerical-computing reflection

Working through this assignment showed me why computational reproducibility is more than saving code that runs once. A clean execution means that the entire analysis can start with the original data and run in the intended order without relying on values left over from an earlier session. Hidden notebook state is risky because a result may appear correct even when it depends on a variable created in a cell that is no longer present or was executed out of order. By keeping the data loading, matrix construction, model fitting, and diagnostics in one Quarto document, I can check that the report is generated from the same code that produces its results.

The matrix computations also helped me distinguish mathematical formulas from good numerical implementations. Although least-squares coefficients can be written as an expression involving the inverse of $(X^\top X)$, explicitly computing that inverse is not necessary and can cause numerical difficulties, especially when the columns of the design matrix are nearly dependent. Using $np.linalg.lstsq()$ is a more reliable approach to solving the least-squares problem. I also learned why $np.allclose()$ is used to check QR and SVD reconstructions: floating-point arithmetic introduces small rounding differences, so exact element-by-element equality is too strict for these checks.

Comparing the condition numbers also showed me why numerical diagnostics are necessary even when a model produces reasonable coefficient estimates. The condition number was much higher before standardization, suggesting that differences in measurement scales contributed substantially to the poor conditioning of the raw design matrix. After the predictors were centered and scaled, the condition number decreased considerably, while the matrix retained full column rank. This suggested that severe near-redundancy was not apparent in this dataset, although standardization cannot eliminate genuine multicollinearity. For my final project, I intend to keep the original data unchanged, organize my files using a consistent project structure, and use relative paths throughout the analysis. I will also render the report from a clean session before submitting it to ensure that the results can be reproduced without relying on hidden notebook state.
